solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Dicky gave somebody a shiner, we hear (5,3)

indicatorNotes.we hear: what we hear is the sound of the phrase, not its spelling

blocks.note: a shiner is a bruised eye, so giving one means darkening someone's eye with a punch; said quickly, the two words run together

annotation.surface: Someone called Dicky has thumped a person and left them with a black eye.
annotation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a name, the culprit; it is the definition. A dicky, or dicky bow, is a bow tie, and 'blacked eye' run together sounds like BLACK TIE.
annotation.definitionFit: Dicky bow is British slang for a bow tie, and a black bow tie is the defining item of black-tie dress, so the part stands for the whole.

entries.clue: Trademark Yankee spirit (6)

blocks.note: Yankee is Y in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: An American patriotic spirit sold as a registered brand.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Yankee spirit' reads as American grit; spirit is the drink.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: distilled from wine, it is one of the classic spirits alongside gin, whisky and rum.

entries.clue: Discharged arrogant trial witness (6)

indicatorNotes.Discharged: emptied of its charge, its load, so the word loses everything inside

blocks.note: ARROGANT with its contents gone leaves A…T

annotation.surface: A cocky witness has been dismissed from the stand in a court case.
annotation.walkthrough: The courtroom makes 'witness' look like a noun; here it is the verb, to bear witness.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to witness a signature is to vouch for it formally.

entries.clue: Jack the serving-boy (5)

blocks.note: the surface wants a boy's name; the setter means the playing card
an old word for a boy servant, before it came to mean a rogue

annotation.surface: A boy named Jack works as the household's serving-boy.
annotation.walkthrough: Jack looks like the serving-boy's name, and 'the' seems to title him; the two are separate definitions of one old word.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the court card between ten and queen has two names, and the older of them first meant a boy or male servant.

entries.clue: Nice tax breaks? That’s not quite true (7)

indicatorNotes.breaks: the letters are broken up and reset

annotation.surface: Someone doubts a claim that Nice, on the French Riviera, offers tax breaks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tax breaks' is a stock phrase, so 'breaks' hides as a noun; Nice is the French city, not the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A near miss rather than a falsehood: the definition softens 'untrue' with 'not quite', which is exactly the sense of imprecise.

entries.clue: France against trapping a large bird of prey (6)

indicatorNotes.trapping: F and CON close round A and L like a snare

blocks.note: F is the international code for France
L = large, as on clothing sizes
con = against, as in pros and cons

annotation.surface: France objects to catching a big raptor.
annotation.walkthrough: The trap is the pair 'France against', F and CON together, with A and L caught between them.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the peregrine and its kin are the swift hunting raptors of falconry.

entries.clue: Typically bitter Times article on the German leader (9)

blocks.note: bitter is a typical kind of ale

annotation.surface: A sour piece in The Times newspaper about the leader of Germany.
annotation.walkthrough: The Times looks like the newspaper, so 'German leader' reads as one phrase; it splits, with 'the German' the article and 'leader' the definition. Bitter is the British name for a hoppy beer.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Alexander the Great, the Macedonian king, is the archetypal military leader.

entries.clue: One dishing out chips at the table? (8)

annotation.definition: One dishing out chips at the table?

blocks.note: the surface wants someone serving fried potatoes; the setter means gaming chips handed out as winnings
not a dining table but a roulette or card table in a casino

annotation.surface: Someone serving fried potatoes at a dinner table.
annotation.walkthrough: Chips at the table suggest a meal, and in Britain chips are fries; the question mark flags that they are casino chips.
annotation.definitionFit: The casino employee who runs a gaming table collects stakes and pays out winnings in chips.

entries.clue: New import started by leading couple of Northampton cobblers (8)

indicatorNotes.leading couple of: the two letters that lead the word, its first two
indicatorNotes.started by: NO goes at the start of the rest

blocks.note: the first two letters of NORTHAMPTON
the import of words is their sense or meaning

annotation.surface: Shoemakers in Northampton begin with a new foreign import.
annotation.walkthrough: Northampton is famous for shoemaking, so cobblers look like its craftsmen. Import is the noun meaning significance, not trade.
annotation.definitionFit: A British slang sense: cobblers, from rhyming slang 'cobbler's awls' for balls, means rubbish talk.

entries.clue: Pest controller visiting ristorante at Ercolano? (8)

indicatorNotes.visiting: a visitor stays inside someone else's place, as the answer stays inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the Italian word for restaurant, through 'at', into the start of the town's name

annotation.surface: An exterminator calls at an Italian restaurant in Ercolano, near Naples.
annotation.walkthrough: The Italian words are there only to hold the letters: ristor(ANTE AT ER)colano.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful description: an animal that lives on ants and termites keeps those pests down, hence the question mark.

entries.clue: Head doctor stops to grieve (6)

indicatorNotes.stops: to stop a gap is to plug it, so the doctor plugs the middle of the head

blocks.note: bean is slang for the head

annotation.surface: A senior doctor ceases mourning.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head doctor' reads as one senior person, and 'stops' as ceasing; the head is the container and the doctor is put inside it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to lament or mourn over a loss, with bemoan usually taking an object.

entries.clue: Hastily study introduction to computer memory (4)

indicatorNotes.introduction to: a word's introduction is its opening, its first letter

annotation.surface: A student swots up on the basics of computer memory in a hurry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Introduction to computer memory' sounds like a course title; it is the first letter of 'computer' and then the memory.
annotation.definitionFit: The word pictures stuffing facts into your head the night before an exam, which is hasty study.

entries.clue: Paris: dire, ramshackle state of dilapidation (9)

indicatorNotes.ramshackle: tumbledown, so the letters fall into a new order

annotation.surface: A gloomy verdict that Paris is dreadful and falling to pieces.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ramshackle' fits the definition's theme, so it seems part of it, but it does the rearranging.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a building left unrepaired until it crumbles is dilapidated.

entries.clue: Fruit marked with spots after peeling (5)

indicatorNotes.after peeling: peeling takes off the skin, here the outer letters of the word

blocks.note: the first and last letters come off

annotation.surface: A piece of fruit found to be blemished once its skin is removed.
annotation.walkthrough: Peeling belongs so naturally to fruit that it passes for part of the picture; it strips the outer letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the commonest orchard fruit.

entries.clue: Duke, most eminent, ignores King (4)

indicatorNotes.ignores: to ignore someone is to leave them out, so the king is left out

annotation.surface: The highest-ranking duke snubs the king.
annotation.walkthrough: Duke looks like a nobleman, to match 'King'; 'put up your dukes' means raise your fists.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang sense, usually plural: dukes are the hands made into fists for a fight.

entries.clue: Running oil rig with Mob complicated business (9)

indicatorNotes.Running: the letters run about into a new order

annotation.surface: Organised crime is operating an oil platform, which is a murky business.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Running' reads as operating the rig; it scrambles the letters. 'with' only joins the definition on.
annotation.definitionFit: A borrowing from Italian for an entanglement: a confused, messy situation hard to get out of.

entries.clue: Camden group regularly dances during religious service (7)

indicatorNotes.regularly: at regular intervals, so every other letter of dances
indicatorNotes.during: one thing happening during another sits inside it

blocks.note: D, N, E: the first, third and fifth letters of DANCES

annotation.surface: A London band dances in rhythm at a church service.
annotation.walkthrough: Camden is a district of north London; its group is a band, not a council committee.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the ska-pop band behind 'Our House' formed in Camden Town in the 1970s.

entries.clue: Want to get on the rocks? You’ll need these (3,5)

annotation.definition: Want to get on the rocks? You’ll need these

blocks.clueFragment: Want to get on the rocks?
blocks.note: the surface suggests wrecking a ship or a marriage; the setter means a drink served over ice
the things the drink is poured over

annotation.surface: A warning to someone who seems bent on wrecking their ship or marriage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On the rocks' suggests shipwreck or a failing marriage; it is the barman's phrase for a drink poured over ice.
annotation.definitionFit: A whisky on the rocks is poured over frozen blocks of water, so they are what the rocks are.

entries.clue: In the morning, brothers served up first-class delicious food (8)

indicatorNotes.served up: in a down clue, sending something up turns it upside down

blocks.note: A1 = first-class, with the 1 read as the letter I, then turned over

annotation.surface: Some brothers bring up a fine breakfast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Served up' fits the food so well it hides that it only turns A1 upside down, the digit 1 standing in as the letter I.
annotation.definitionFit: Ambrosia was the food of the Greek gods, so by extension anything delicious to eat.

entries.clue: Temporary sleeping accommodation affected teaching grad (4-3)

blocks.note: a BEd is a Bachelor of Education

annotation.surface: A newly qualified teacher with a mannered style is lodged somewhere for the time being.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Affected' reads as emotionally moved; it means mannered. The graduate is the degree itself.
annotation.definitionFit: The folding bed put up for a guest or on a trip is sleeping accommodation meant for a night or two.

entries.clue: Clubs backing out of transfer agreement (4)

indicatorNotes.backing out of: to back out of something is to withdraw from it, so C leaves the word

blocks.note: a decal is a transfer, a picture applied to a surface
C = clubs, the card suit; removed

annotation.surface: Football clubs withdraw from a player transfer deal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' tempts a reversal, but it is backing out, withdrawal. The transfer is a stick-on picture, not a football move.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a business arrangement agreed by both sides.

entries.clue: Retired dull Welsh versifier (4)

indicatorNotes.Retired: to retire is to draw back, so the word goes backwards

annotation.surface: A tedious Welsh poet who has stopped working.
annotation.walkthrough: Retired reads as having left work; it is the reversal instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Welsh tradition gives its poets this title, still honoured at the Eisteddfod festival.

entries.clue: Little ‘un, alone, exposed in the old city (7)

indicatorNotes.exposed: stripped of its covering, so the outer letters go

blocks.note: ALONE without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A small child is left alone and unprotected in an ancient city.
annotation.walkthrough: The abandoned child is a picture only; exposing ALONE strips its outer letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Mesopotamian capital of Nebuchadnezzar is one of the most famous ancient cities.

entries.clue: Firm employing no good family member (6)

indicatorNotes.no: 'no good' means without good, so the G for good is taken away

blocks.note: USING = employing, less G for good

annotation.surface: A company that hires a useless relative.
annotation.walkthrough: 'No good' reads as useless; it asks for G to be removed.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the child of an aunt or uncle is one kind of relative.

entries.clue: Guard key soldiers back in Aldershot (6)

indicatorNotes.back in: the letter at the back of Aldershot

blocks.note: the Escape key on a keyboard
OR = other ranks, soldiers who aren't officers

annotation.surface: Key soldiers are back guarding the garrison town of Aldershot.
annotation.walkthrough: Aldershot is the home of the British Army, which keeps the surface military. 'Back' tempts a reversal of the soldiers; it only takes the last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, noun or verb: an armed escort guards whoever it accompanies.

entries.clue: Load front of container ship skippered by Jason (5)

indicatorNotes.front of: the letter at the front of container

blocks.note: Jason's ship in the Greek myth of the Golden Fleece

annotation.surface: Instructions to fill a container ship captained by someone called Jason.
annotation.walkthrough: Jason sounds like a modern captain; he is the Jason of myth, whose crew were the Argonauts.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the goods a ship or plane carries are its load.

entries.clue: It hinders cricketer getting run in a defeat (9)

annotation.definitionNote: a clause standing for the noun: an albatross is something that hinders

indicatorNotes.in: the cricketer and run are placed in the defeat

annotation.surface: A cricketer who scores a run despite the side losing is still a drag on the team.
annotation.walkthrough: The cricket is all wordplay: the batsman and his run go inside the second word, the defeat, after A. In golf the same word is a score, but here it is the burden.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: in Coleridge's 'Ancient Mariner' the dead bird hung round the sailor's neck, so the word means a burden that hinders.

entries.clue: Sailor unloaded outermost deck (5)

indicatorNotes.unloaded: the contents of outermost are taken out, leaving its ends

annotation.surface: A sailor has cleared the furthest deck of a ship.
annotation.walkthrough: The sailor puts 'deck' on a ship; it is a pack of cards.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the fortune-teller's pack is one kind of deck of cards.

entries.clue: Broke edges of lace undergarment (6)

indicatorNotes.edges of: just the two outside letters of lace

blocks.note: first and last letters of LACE

annotation.surface: The lace trim of a piece of underwear has torn.
annotation.walkthrough: Broke reads as a verb, tore; it is the adjective, skint.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Victorian pad or frame worn under a skirt to puff it out behind.

entries.clue: Languedoc serf Lafarge sent back outside in the fresh air (8)

indicatorNotes.sent back: what is sent back returns the way it came, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: the letters span the end of the region, all of 'serf' and the start of the surname; read them right to left

annotation.surface: A peasant named Lafarge in Languedoc, a region of southern France, is sent back out into the open air.
annotation.walkthrough: The French names only carry the letters: languED(OC SERF LA)farge, backwards. Nothing announces the hiding, so the tight run of letters must.
annotation.definitionFit: A borrowing from Italian, literally 'in the fresh', used for eating or acting outdoors.

entries.clue: Dog commercial featured in TV programme (6)

indicatorNotes.featured in: an item featured in a programme appears within it, so one word sits inside the other

annotation.surface: A dog appears in an advert shown during a TV programme.
annotation.walkthrough: Dog looks like the animal star of the advert; it is the verb, to follow closely.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to dog someone's footsteps is to trail them closely.

entries.clue: Gut feeling mum ignored in Main Street in Connecticut (8)

indicatorNotes.ignored: what is ignored is left out, so mum's letters drop from the word

annotation.surface: A mother's hunch goes unheeded on Main Street in a Connecticut town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Main Street' reads as one American place name; it splits, with mum removed from the first word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: knowing without reasoning, felt in the gut rather than worked out.
